artifact.recommendation: Adopt a managed search service behind an internal abstraction and a portable, vendor-neutral index pipeline.
reasoning: It is the only option that credibly meets the four-month launch deadline while providing faceting, typo tolerance, and near-real-time indexing.

Building immediately is inconsistent with current staffing: the backend team is at capacity, operations cannot add on-call headcount, and the cluster would require a rotating primary owner plus upgrade work.
The internal prototype required six engineer-weeks yet delivered only basic keyword search, indicating substantial remaining delivery risk for an in-house build.
Delaying for hiring would threaten the contracted design-partner expansion and is unnecessary because search relevance is important but not a core differentiator.
Vendor risk is manageable: canonical search documents, an internal abstraction, and bulk export support provide the foundations for migration.
The projected first-year cost is material but proportionate at 7 percent of the product infrastructure budget, given the avoided staffing and delay costs.
considerations: Keep query and indexing interfaces internal; prevent vendor-specific response models, ranking controls, and identifiers from leaking into product code.
Store canonical documents and source-of-truth data outside the search vendor, and make indexes reproducible rather than authoritative.
Build export/reindex tooling early and test restoration into a non-vendor-specific target or representative open-source engine.
Define relevance, indexing-latency, availability, and cost thresholds before signing the contract.
Negotiate data portability, deletion, rate limits, price protections, incident support, and termination assistance.
Reassess build-versus-buy when scale, cost, relevance differentiation, or staffing materially changes.
assumptions: The managed service can satisfy required security, privacy, residency, availability, and procurement requirements within four months.
Its near-real-time indexing performance meets the product's actual latency target at expected traffic.
The 7 percent estimate includes realistic query, indexing, storage, replica, support, and data-transfer charges.
A six-month delay would exceed the four-month requirement and jeopardize the design-partner expansion.
The canonical search document contains enough information to rebuild equivalent indexes elsewhere.
risks: Vendor-specific ranking behavior or advanced features may create semantic lock-in despite API abstraction.
Usage growth, replicas, analytics, or transfer fees could make managed-service costs rise faster than projected.
Bulk export alone may be insufficient for rapid migration if ranking configuration, synonyms, facets, typo settings, and operational metadata are not portable.
An abstraction designed too broadly could slow delivery; one designed too narrowly could fail to provide a practical exit path.
Service outages, throttling, regional limitations, or vendor roadmap changes could affect product reliability.
Procurement or security review could consume enough schedule to threaten the launch.
evidence_needed: Load-test results for indexing latency, query latency, typo tolerance, faceting, and relevance on representative data and traffic.
A complete three-year total-cost model, including growth scenarios, support, replicas, transfers, and migration costs.
A proof-of-portability that exports canonical data and rebuilds a usable index in an alternative engine within a defined recovery objective.
Contract and architecture review covering data ownership, export completeness, deletion, rate limits, SLAs, regional availability, and termination terms.
A delivery plan showing procurement, integration, relevance tuning, observability, and contingency milestones inside four months.
Explicit acceptance metrics for relevance quality and near-real-time indexing.

Store canonical search documents and indexing checkpoints outside the vendor so indexes can be rebuilt elsewhere without reconstructing source data.
Treat the documented bulk export API as a supplementary exit mechanism, not the sole migration strategy.
Define relevance metrics, latency and freshness objectives, failure handling, data residency requirements, and spend alerts before contracting.
Run an early migration rehearsal by rebuilding a representative index in an alternative engine and documenting estimated switching time and cost.
assumptions: The managed service's near-real-time indexing performance satisfies the product's freshness requirement at expected traffic.
The four-month timeline includes procurement, security review, integration, relevance tuning, and production hardening.
The projected 7 percent infrastructure-budget cost is acceptable and includes realistic query, indexing, storage, and data-transfer usage.
The canonical search document can express all required facets and relevance fields without vendor-specific source transformations.
risks: Query semantics, ranking controls, analytics, synonyms, and typo-tolerance behavior may remain vendor-specific despite an internal abstraction.
Pricing may rise materially with traffic, replicas, storage, or premium feature usage.
Export capability alone may not preserve ranking configuration, operational metadata, or equivalent behavior in another engine.
A thinly staffed backend team may still face integration and relevance-tuning pressure within the launch window.
Vendor outages, service limits, or procurement delays could threaten launch unless mitigated early.

A complete cost model with growth scenarios, overage pricing, replicas, retention, data transfer, and premium features.
Contract review covering data portability, export throughput, termination assistance, price-change terms, service levels, and data deletion.

citations.claim: The internal prototype required six engineer-weeks but delivered only basic keyword search without typo tolerance or faceting.
The managed service supports all launch requirements and provides a documented bulk export API.
Projected year-one managed-service spend is 7 percent of the product infrastructure budget.
Operating an open-source cluster would require rotating primary on-call ownership and quarterly upgrades.

strengths: The recommendation directly addresses the deadline, feature, staffing, on-call, and portability constraints.
The reasoning is well grounded in the supplied evidence, especially the prototype shortfall, managed-service capabilities, operational burden, and canonical document model.
The proposed narrow abstraction avoids the common mistake of building an overly broad portability layer.
Storing canonical documents and checkpoints independently is a stronger migration strategy than relying on vendor export alone.
The report identifies important residual lock-in in ranking, query semantics, synonyms, analytics, and typo-tolerance behavior.
The requested proof of concept, load testing, cost modeling, contract review, and timed portability rehearsal are concrete and decision-relevant.
weaknesses: Calling managed search the “only option” that can credibly meet the deadline is stronger than the evidence establishes; no delivery estimate for a production open-source implementation is provided.
The conclusion that managed-service cost is “proportionate” relies only on its share of the infrastructure budget, without comparing it to value, alternatives, or future traffic scenarios.
The report does not prioritize its evidence-needed items or identify which are contracting gates versus post-selection safeguards.
The recommendation does not define acceptance thresholds for relevance, latency, freshness, availability, cost, or migration time.
The stated confidence of 0.97 is excessive given the number of unresolved assumptions and potentially launch-blocking unknowns.
unsupported: The claim that delaying for dedicated hires is “unnecessary” is a judgment not fully demonstrated by the supplied evidence.
The claim that delaying for hires risks the contracted expansion extrapolates from evidence about a six-month delay; the hiring option has no specified delay duration.
The assumption that procurement, security review, integration, tuning, and hardening all fit within four months is not supported by the evidence.
The assumption that 7 percent includes realistic query, indexing, storage, replication, premium-feature, and transfer charges is unverified.
The claim that canonical documents plus an adapter preserve a practical migration path remains unproven until query behavior, ranking configuration, and rebuild duration are tested.
missing: A weighted comparison of all three options against deadline, capability, staffing, operational burden, cost, and portability criteria.
A quantified total-cost-of-ownership comparison covering engineering labor, incident response, upgrades, managed-service charges, and expected growth.
Explicit launch acceptance criteria for relevance quality, typo tolerance, facet correctness, indexing freshness, latency, and availability.
A contingency plan if procurement, security review, vendor integration, or load testing fails to meet the schedule.
A defined fallback engine and evidence that it can ingest the canonical schema and reproduce critical query behavior.
Security, privacy, compliance, tenant-isolation, data-residency, retention, and deletion requirements specific to indexed data.
Ownership for relevance tuning, schema evolution, incident response, vendor escalation, and portability rehearsals despite the backend team being at capacity.
Contract and architecture controls for API limits, throttling, outage behavior, retries, backfills, dual writes, and index rebuilds.
incorrect_assumptions: A documented bulk export API should not be assumed to provide timely or complete portability; the report appropriately warns about this but still depends on portability remaining practical.
Vendor-neutral source documents do not make query logic, ranking, analyzers, synonyms, facets, or operational procedures vendor-neutral.
Feature availability does not establish acceptable relevance, performance, limits, or production readiness at expected traffic.
A managed service reduces infrastructure operations but does not eliminate on-call demand for application integration, indexing failures, relevance regressions, or vendor outages.
critical_risks: Procurement or security-review delay could invalidate the central four-month feasibility argument.
The capacity-constrained backend team may be unable to complete integration, relevance tuning, hardening, and migration safeguards concurrently.
Unexpected pricing at scale or dependence on premium features could turn the favorable year-one estimate into significant lock-in.
Nonportable ranking and query behavior could make a nominal rebuild technically possible but commercially impractical.
Failure to establish measurable relevance and freshness thresholds could allow a feature-complete but poor search experience to launch.
Vendor outages, service quotas, or insufficient export throughput could threaten availability or make exit timelines unacceptable.
recommended_changes: Replace “only option” with “best-supported option based on current evidence” unless delivery estimates eliminate the alternatives.
Make adoption conditional on a time-boxed proof of concept, security and procurement feasibility, a complete cost model, and a timed rebuild into a named alternative engine.
Define numeric acceptance thresholds for relevance, p95/p99 latency, indexing freshness, availability, peak throughput, annual cost, and maximum migration duration.
Add a decision matrix comparing all options and include engineering labor and operational burden in total cost.
Separate pre-contract decision gates from post-contract implementation controls and assign owners and deadlines.
Document a schedule contingency, including the latest viable procurement date and a reduced-scope or fallback launch plan.
Lower confidence to reflect unresolved feasibility, cost, relevance, and portability evidence; approximately 0.8 would be more defensible before validation.

strengths: The recommendation directly addresses the four-month deadline, required search capabilities, staffing limits, and migration-path constraint.

The reasoning is traceable to the supplied evidence, with accurate citations for the prototype outcome, managed-service capabilities, estimated cost, operational burden, delay impact, and canonical document model.

The report recognizes that API abstraction alone does not eliminate semantic lock-in and specifically identifies ranking configuration, synonyms, facets, typo settings, and metadata as portability concerns.

The implementation considerations are practical: retain an external source of truth, make indexes reproducible, isolate vendor models, test reindexing, define service thresholds, and negotiate termination terms.
The evidence-needed section appropriately treats security, procurement, performance, relevance, total cost, contractual protections, and portability as validation gates rather than settled facts.
The report sensibly recommends reassessing the decision if scale, economics, strategic relevance, or staffing changes.
weaknesses: The confidence of 0.96 is too high because several potentially decision-blocking matters remain unverified, including procurement timing, security compliance, workload performance, three-year cost, and migration feasibility.
The option comparison is qualitative and incomplete; it does not provide estimated schedules, staffing requirements, total costs, or failure probabilities for all three options.

The report does not clearly distinguish launch-critical abstraction work from portability work that could be staged after launch, despite acknowledging that an overly broad abstraction may delay delivery.
The recommendation lacks explicit go/no-go criteria and a dated fallback plan if procurement, security review, integration, or load testing fails.
The cost discussion relies heavily on the percentage of the infrastructure budget without comparing it with revenue impact, absolute spend, alternative operating cost, or growth sensitivity.
unsupported: Calling managed search the only option that credibly meets the deadline is plausible but not established by an implementation plan or schedule estimate for each option.
The claim that delaying for hiring is unnecessary is a judgment not demonstrated by evidence about hiring timelines, future relevance needs, or organizational strategy.

Characterizing 7 percent of the infrastructure budget as proportionate is unsupported without absolute cost, budget priorities, growth scenarios, and comparison against internal labor and opportunity costs.

The statement that canonical documents, abstraction, and bulk export make vendor risk manageable is premature without proving configuration portability and successful reconstruction in another engine.
The report connects the delay option to a six-month delay, but the option itself only says to delay until dedicated engineers can be hired; no hiring duration is supplied.
Avoided staffing costs are asserted but not quantified, and managed adoption will still require integration, tuning, monitoring, incident response, and vendor-management labor.
missing: A weighted decision matrix comparing capability fit, four-month deliverability, operational load, lock-in, cost, reliability, and reversibility across all options.
A critical-path delivery estimate covering procurement, security review, data pipeline work, frontend/backend integration, relevance tuning, observability, and launch readiness.
Quantified acceptance thresholds for indexing freshness, query latency, relevance, availability, recovery, export throughput, and migration duration.
Representative workload details, including document count and size, update rate, query volume, facet cardinality, traffic growth, and geographic requirements.
An explicit ownership model for managed-service incidents, relevance tuning, schema evolution, cost monitoring, and vendor escalation under the fixed on-call constraint.
A fallback strategy if the preferred vendor fails security review, procurement, performance testing, or contract negotiation, including the latest safe decision date.
Evaluation of whether a thinner launch scope could reduce schedule or vendor dependence while still satisfying contractual and product needs.
A three-year financial comparison including internal engineering labor, operational overhead, support tiers, replicas, transfer fees, growth, migration work, and delay costs.
incorrect_assumptions: The assumption that a six-month delay necessarily represents the hiring option is not grounded in the option description; hiring could take less or more time.

The report implicitly treats a documented bulk export API as meaningful portability, although export completeness, throughput, format, configuration coverage, and contractual availability are unknown.

The assumption that a canonical search document can support equivalent indexes elsewhere may fail if relevance depends on proprietary analyzers, ranking behavior, typo algorithms, analytics, or configuration.
The recommendation appears to assume that existing staff can absorb managed-service integration and operational ownership even though the backend team is already at capacity.
critical_risks: Security, privacy, residency, or procurement failure could invalidate the preferred option late enough to miss the four-month launch.
Semantic lock-in may remain substantial even with portable documents if product behavior becomes dependent on proprietary ranking, analysis, typo handling, personalization, or analytics.
Unmodeled growth and ancillary charges could make the service materially more expensive than the year-one estimate.
A nominal migration path may be operationally unusable if export and reindexing cannot meet an agreed recovery or transition objective.
The managed service still creates incident-response and operational work; without named ownership, the no-additional-on-call constraint could produce reliability gaps.
Building too much abstraction and portability tooling before launch could consume the schedule advantage that motivates the managed-service choice.
recommended_changes: Lower confidence to reflect unresolved decision gates; approximately 0.78–0.85 would better match the current evidence.
Make the recommendation conditional on security, procurement, representative load testing, contract terms, and a three-year cost ceiling passing by explicit dates.
Add a concise decision matrix with comparable schedule, staffing, cost, operational burden, capability, and exit-risk estimates for every option.
Define a minimal launch abstraction focused on canonical input, stable internal query contracts, and vendor-model containment; schedule broader portability only where it protects a tested exit path.
Require a time-boxed proof of portability that rebuilds representative data and essential search behavior in an alternative engine within a stated objective.
Quantify all launch acceptance criteria and assign owners for integration, relevance, operations, cost control, and vendor incidents.
Create a contingency plan with a latest decision date and fallback vendor or reduced-scope launch if procurement or validation fails.
Replace claims that cost is proportionate and lock-in is manageable with conditional language until financial modeling and migration testing support them.

attacks: The managed-service recommendation assumes the capacity-constrained backend team can absorb procurement, integration, relevance tuning, observability, incident handling, and portability work; managed infrastructure reduces cluster operations but does not solve the stated staffing constraint.

Calling managed search the only credible four-month option is unsubstantiated because no critical-path schedule or comparable estimate exists for any option, including a reduced-scope open-source launch.

The recommendation treats feature availability as evidence of production fitness, but there is no representative proof of relevance, freshness, latency, facet correctness, throughput, quotas, or availability.

The claimed practical migration path is largely architectural intent. Canonical documents and API abstraction do not port analyzers, ranking behavior, typo algorithms, synonyms, query semantics, analytics, or operating procedures.

The bulk export API is weak evidence of reversibility without verified completeness, throughput, configuration coverage, contractual availability after termination, and a timed rebuild into a named alternative.

The 7 percent year-one estimate cannot support the claim that cost is proportionate: absolute spend, growth sensitivity, premium features, replicas, support, transfers, labor, and migration costs are absent.
The delay option is dismissed using evidence about a six-month delay even though no hiring duration is given; the causal link to losing the design-partner expansion is therefore incomplete.

The proposal may erase its schedule advantage by requiring abstraction, export tooling, a portability rehearsal, hardening, and contract negotiation before launch, yet it does not separate launch gates from deferrable safeguards.

No named owner exists for relevance, schema changes, indexing failures, cost controls, vendor escalation, or application on-call, making the recommendation potentially incompatible with the no-new-on-call constraint.
Confidence near 0.97 is indefensible while procurement, security, workload performance, staffing feasibility, total cost, and migration viability remain unresolved and potentially decision-reversing.
falsifiers: A dated delivery plan shows procurement, security review, integration, relevance tuning, observability, and production hardening cannot complete within four months using currently available staff.
Representative testing fails predefined thresholds for relevance, typo tolerance, facet correctness, p95/p99 query latency, indexing freshness, peak throughput, or availability.
Security, privacy, residency, retention, deletion, tenant-isolation, or procurement review rejects the service or cannot finish by the latest safe decision date.
A staffing model shows managed integration and ongoing incident ownership require additional on-call capacity or displace launch-critical backend work.
A three-year cost model exceeds an agreed ceiling under credible traffic, replica, support, analytics, storage, or transfer scenarios.
A timed migration rehearsal cannot reproduce essential search behavior in a named alternative engine within the required transition objective.
Vendor contracts do not guarantee usable export throughput, data/configuration access, deletion, termination assistance, pricing protections, or continued access during exit.
The product's required relevance depends materially on proprietary ranking, analyzers, typo handling, personalization, or analytics that the internal contract cannot represent portably.

A scoped open-source or alternative managed implementation demonstrates equal launch capability within four months with acceptable staffing and operational burden, disproving the claim that the preferred option is uniquely feasible.
The design-partner agreement does not actually require the proposed search scope or tolerate no reduced-scope launch, weakening the central opportunity-cost argument.
evidence_gaps: Comparable critical-path schedules, staffing allocations, costs, and failure probabilities for all three options.
Representative document volume, update rate, query load, facet cardinality, geographic distribution, growth, and service-limit requirements.
Numeric launch criteria for relevance, typo quality, facet correctness, freshness, latency, availability, recovery, and throughput.
A named accountable owner and capacity budget for integration, tuning, schema evolution, incidents, cost monitoring, and vendor management.
Completed security, privacy, compliance, residency, retention, deletion, procurement, and legal assessments.
A three-year total-cost comparison including internal labor, support tiers, replicas, premium features, transfers, growth, incident work, migration, and delay costs.
A proof that the canonical schema captures every field and transformation needed to rebuild critical search behavior outside the vendor.
A timed rebuild into a named fallback engine, including configuration translation, validation, cutover, rollback, and acceptable behavior differences.
Verified export completeness, formats, rate limits, throughput, costs, termination-period access, and coverage of synonyms, ranking rules, facets, and metadata.
A dated contingency plan with a latest viable vendor commitment date and fallback vendor, reduced-scope launch, or contractual workaround.
Evidence connecting the hiring option to a six-month delay and quantifying the probability and value of losing the design-partner expansion.
A definition of which abstraction and portability controls are mandatory before launch versus safely staged afterward.

accepted_criticisms: The managed-service option still requires procurement, integration, relevance tuning, observability, incident ownership, and vendor management; the original report did not demonstrate that the capacity-constrained team can absorb this work.
The assertion that managed search is the only credible four-month option is unsupported without comparable critical-path estimates, including a reduced-scope open-source alternative.
Feature availability and a documented API do not establish production fitness; representative tests and numeric acceptance thresholds are required.
Canonical documents and an internal API reduce data and application coupling but do not make analyzers, ranking, typo behavior, synonyms, analytics, or operating procedures portable.

A bulk export API is insufficient evidence of practical reversibility without validating completeness, throughput, configuration coverage, termination access, and reconstruction in a named alternative.
The 7 percent year-one estimate does not establish proportionate cost without absolute spend, growth scenarios, ancillary charges, labor, and migration costs.
The evidence about a six-month delay does not establish that waiting to hire would cause a six-month delay.
Launch-critical abstraction work was not separated from safeguards that can be staged, so portability work could consume the managed option's schedule advantage.
The recommendation needs named owners and capacity allocations for relevance, schema evolution, indexing failures, cost control, vendor escalation, and application incidents.
Confidence of 0.96 was too high given unresolved procurement, security, performance, staffing, cost, and migration gates.
The recommendation needs explicit go/no-go criteria, a latest safe decision date, and a fallback vendor or reduced-scope launch plan.
rejected_criticisms: The criticism that managed service should not be recommended at all is not supported by the visible evidence. It remains the leading option because it supplies the required features while immediate self-operation explicitly adds primary on-call and upgrade work, both poorly aligned with the stated constraints.

A full weighted decision matrix is not necessary to make a provisional recommendation from the supplied evidence, although comparable schedules, staffing, and costs are necessary before treating that recommendation as final.

A pre-launch migration rehearsal need not reproduce identical proprietary behavior; a practical exit path may allow documented, acceptable behavior differences. It must, however, prove that essential behavior and data can be rebuilt within an agreed transition objective.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Provisionally select managed search behind a minimal internal query/indexing boundary and a vendor-neutral canonical document pipeline, but authorize commitment only if dated security and procurement reviews, representative performance and relevance tests, an explicit staffing/on-call ownership model, acceptable contract and export terms, and a three-year cost ceiling pass by a latest safe decision date. Keep canonical source data outside the vendor. Before launch, implement only the containment needed to prevent vendor models from leaking into product code; time-box a rebuild into a named alternative and stage noncritical portability tooling if necessary. Define a fallback vendor or reduced-scope launch if any gate fails. Do not claim that managed search is uniquely feasible until alternatives have comparable delivery estimates.
reasons: The supplied evidence favors managed search over immediate self-operation: the prototype remained incomplete after six engineer-weeks, while operating an open-source cluster requires primary on-call ownership and upgrades.
Managed search directly supports the required launch features, but availability on a feature list is not proof that it satisfies the product's workload, quality, security, or schedule requirements.
The canonical document model and external source of truth materially reduce data lock-in, yet semantic and operational portability remain unproven.
The delay option conflicts with the four-month launch requirement, but the claimed connection between hiring and a six-month delay is not established.
The original recommendation's direction remains reasonable, but its exclusivity, cost characterization, lock-in characterization, and confidence exceeded the visible evidence.

accepted_criticisms: “Only option that credibly meets the four-month deadline” is too strong without comparable critical-path schedules and staffing estimates.
Managed-service feature availability does not establish production fitness; representative relevance, correctness, freshness, latency, throughput, quota, and availability testing is required.
Managed infrastructure reduces cluster operations but still requires capacity and ownership for integration, tuning, indexing failures, incidents, cost controls, and vendor escalation.
Canonical documents and a narrow adapter reduce data-model lock-in but do not make analyzers, ranking, typo handling, synonyms, query semantics, analytics, or operating procedures portable.

A documented bulk export API is insufficient evidence of reversibility without validating completeness, throughput, configuration coverage, termination access, and a timed rebuild into a named alternative.
The 7 percent year-one estimate does not establish proportionate total cost without absolute spend, growth scenarios, premium features, replicas, transfers, support, labor, and migration costs.
The hiring-delay argument improperly extrapolates from evidence about a six-month delay when the actual hiring timeline is unspecified.
The report fails to distinguish launch-critical gates from portability and hardening safeguards that may be staged after launch.
The absence of named owners and capacity budgets is a material gap under the no-new-on-call constraint.
Confidence of 0.97 is excessive given unresolved schedule, procurement, security, workload, staffing, cost, and portability questions.
rejected_criticisms: The criticism that the recommendation simply assumes managed-service work is absorbable overstates the report: it explicitly identifies integration and relevance-tuning pressure as a risk and treats four-month completion as an assumption requiring validation.

The criticism that the report treats bulk export as its primary migration mechanism is inaccurate; it explicitly calls export supplementary and prioritizes independently retained canonical documents and checkpoints.
The criticism that the report presents canonical documents and abstraction as proven portability is overstated; the report acknowledges nonportable behavior and calls for a timed portability test.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Select managed search as the best-supported option, but make commitment conditional on time-boxed representative testing, security and procurement clearance, a staffed delivery plan with named operational owners, a three-year cost model, and a timed rebuild into a named fallback engine. Define numeric launch thresholds and a latest viable commitment date with a reduced-scope contingency. Stage nonessential portability work after launch where doing so does not compromise the practical exit path.
reasons: The supplied evidence still favors managed search: it provides the required features, while the internal prototype remained incomplete after six engineer-weeks and open-source operation requires on-call ownership that conflicts with stated constraints.
The canonical document model provides a credible foundation for data portability, although behavioral and operational portability remain unproven.
Delay remains commercially risky because a six-month delay would lose a contracted expansion, but the evidence does not establish that hiring necessarily causes that delay.
The recommendation remains directionally sound, so no position change is warranted; the needed correction is to make it conditional, remove exclusivity and cost overclaims, and lower confidence.
Several unresolved issues could reverse the decision or invalidate the deadline, making 0.80 more defensible than 0.97.

artifact.decision: Provisionally choose the managed search service, subject to explicit feasibility gates; do not yet authorize an unconditional vendor commitment.
artifact.action: Run a time-boxed validation phase with a latest safe commitment date. Require representative quality and load tests, completed security/procurement review, named delivery and operational owners with capacity allocations, acceptable contract/export terms, a three-year cost ceiling, and a timed rebuild into a named fallback engine. Use only a minimal internal query/indexing boundary and retain canonical source documents outside the vendor. Prepare a fallback vendor or reduced-scope launch if any gate fails.
reasons: Managed search is the best-supported option because it already offers the required features, whereas the internal prototype remained incomplete after six engineer-weeks.
Immediate open-source operation conflicts most directly with the staffing constraints because it requires rotating primary on-call ownership and quarterly upgrades.
Managed infrastructure still requires integration, tuning, monitoring, incident response, and vendor management; current team capacity to perform that work is unproven.
The evidence establishes feature availability, not production fitness for the representative workload.
Canonical documents and an internal boundary reduce data and application coupling, but behavioral and operational portability remain unproven.
The four-month deadline makes waiting unattractive, but the evidence does not establish how long hiring would take or that it necessarily causes the cited six-month delay.
The 7 percent year-one estimate is insufficient to establish acceptable total cost or cost advantage.
The unresolved issues are potentially decision-reversing, so the selection must remain conditional and confidence should be materially below the researchers' 0.96–0.97.
evidence: Problem e1: the prior prototype used six engineer-weeks and delivered only basic keyword search, without typo tolerance or faceting.
Problem e2: the managed service supports the required launch features and documents a bulk export API.
Problem e4: operating the open-source cluster is estimated to require a rotating primary on-call owner plus quarterly upgrades.
Problem context and constraints: the backend team is already at capacity, launch is required within four months, and operational on-call headcount cannot increase.
Problem e6: the product can emit a vendor-neutral canonical search document before indexing.
Problem e3 supplies only a year-one estimate equal to 7 percent of the product infrastructure budget; it does not supply absolute or multi-year total cost.
Problem e5 establishes the consequence of a six-month delay, but no artifact establishes that hiring would take six months.
rejected_alternatives: Do not immediately build and operate the open-source cluster: the visible evidence shows incomplete prior progress and an operational burden that conflicts with fixed on-call staffing.
Do not delay outright for dedicated hires: that option does not satisfy the stated four-month launch requirement on the current record, although its actual hiring duration remains unknown.
Do not make an unconditional managed-service commitment: staffing feasibility, procurement, security, workload performance, cost, and practical portability have not been demonstrated.
Do not claim managed search is uniquely capable of meeting the deadline: no comparable critical-path estimates exist for managed, reduced-scope open-source, or alternative managed implementations.
Do not require exact cross-engine behavioral equivalence as the migration standard; a practical exit can tolerate documented differences if essential behavior and transition objectives are met.
minority: A reduced-scope open-source launch or another managed vendor could prove equally deliverable within four months; the artifacts contain no comparable schedule to exclude them.
Hiring could take materially less than six months, weakening the commercial case against delay, although delay still conflicts with the stated four-month requirement absent another arrangement.
Some portability tooling may safely be staged after launch, provided minimum vendor containment and a credible exit foundation exist before commitment.
unresolved: Whether procurement, security, privacy, residency, retention, deletion, and legal reviews can finish before the latest safe decision date.
Whether existing staff can absorb integration, relevance tuning, observability, indexing failures, application incidents, cost control, and vendor escalation.
Numeric acceptance thresholds and representative results for relevance, typo tolerance, facet correctness, freshness, p95/p99 latency, throughput, quotas, and availability.
Three-year total cost under realistic growth, replicas, premium features, support, transfers, labor, incidents, and migration scenarios.
Export completeness, throughput, cost, configuration coverage, termination-period access, and contractual protections.
Whether essential ranking, analyzer, synonym, typo, query, and analytics behavior can be rebuilt in a named alternative within an agreed transition objective.
Comparable schedules, staffing requirements, costs, and failure risks for all options.
The actual hiring duration and whether the design-partner expansion requires the full proposed search scope.
Which portability and hardening controls are launch-critical versus safely deferrable.
assumptions: The four-month launch requirement is firm.
The required launch scope includes faceting, typo tolerance, and near-real-time indexing.
A conditional selection can precede final vendor commitment without consuming the fallback window.
Canonical source data can be retained independently of the managed service.
A practical migration path permits documented behavioral differences while preserving essential product behavior and recoverability.
change_conditions: Reject the managed option if security, procurement, or legal clearance cannot complete by the latest safe commitment date.
Reject or rescope it if representative tests miss predefined quality, latency, freshness, throughput, quota, or availability thresholds.

artifact.decision: Provisionally choose managed search behind a minimal internal abstraction and vendor-neutral canonical document pipeline; do not make an irreversible commitment until feasibility gates pass.
artifact.action: Time-box a managed-service validation phase with a latest safe commitment date. Require representative relevance and workload tests, security/procurement clearance, named delivery and incident owners, acceptable contract/export terms, and a three-year cost ceiling. Preserve canonical source data outside the vendor, contain vendor-specific models, test a rebuild into a named fallback engine, and prepare a reduced-scope launch contingency.
reasons: Managed search is the best-supported option because it supplies the required launch features, whereas the prior internal prototype remained incomplete after six engineer-weeks.
Immediate open-source operation conflicts most directly with the fixed on-call constraint because it requires a rotating primary owner and quarterly upgrades.

Managed service reduces cluster-operating work but does not eliminate integration, tuning, observability, incident, cost-control, or vendor-management demands; staff capacity must therefore be an explicit gate.

Canonical documents and an internal boundary reduce data and application coupling, but practical migration remains unproven for ranking, analyzers, typo handling, synonyms, query semantics, and operating procedures.
The four-month feasibility, production fitness, total cost, and exit path are unresolved and could reverse the choice, so the recommendation is conditional rather than final.

Waiting for hires is incompatible with the stated four-month launch unless hiring and delivery can occur within that window; the supplied six-month-loss evidence does not establish the actual hiring duration.
evidence: The launch requires faceting, typo tolerance, and near-real-time indexing within four months.
The managed service supports the required launch features and documents a bulk export API.
The internal prototype delivered only basic keyword search after six engineer-weeks and lacked typo tolerance and faceting.
Operating the open-source cluster is estimated to require rotating primary on-call ownership plus quarterly upgrades, while operational on-call headcount cannot increase.
The backend team is already at capacity.
The product can emit vendor-neutral canonical search documents before indexing, providing a useful—but incomplete—portability foundation.
Projected year-one service spend is 7 percent of the product infrastructure budget, but this alone does not establish affordability or total cost.
A six-month delay is estimated to forgo a contracted design-partner expansion, although no evidence ties hiring to exactly six months.
rejected_alternatives: Build and operate open-source search immediately: currently weaker because the prototype shortfall, team capacity, and explicit on-call burden create substantial deadline and operating conflicts. Reconsider if a scoped implementation demonstrates four-month delivery without additional on-call capacity.
Delay until dedicated engineers are hired: currently fails the explicit four-month launch requirement absent evidence that hiring and implementation can finish within that period.
Unconditionally commit to managed search now: rejected because security, procurement, workload performance, staffing ownership, long-term cost, and migration feasibility have not been validated.
Treat the bulk export API or canonical documents as sufficient portability: rejected because neither proves portable configuration, behavior, throughput, termination access, or transition time.
minority: A reduced-scope open-source launch could be competitive, but no comparable schedule, staffing plan, or capability demonstration is visible.
A managed-service commitment may still be infeasible if existing staff cannot absorb integration and ongoing application-level incident ownership.
